title: Jeremiah 3:19–25
context: In 3:19–20 the LORD speaks of what he desired for his people: a place among the children, a pleasant land, and a relationship in which they would call him “My Father” and not turn away. Instead, like a wife who departs treacherously, the house of Israel has dealt treacherously with him. In 3:21 a voice is heard on the bare heights, the very places of idolatry (3:2), as the children of Israel weep and plead. The LORD calls again, “Return, you backsliding children, and I will heal your backsliding” (3:22a), and the people answer in a confession that runs through 3:25: “Behold, we have come to you; for you are the LORD our God.” Their confession renounces the help of the hills (3:23), names “the shameful thing” that devoured their fathers’ labor (3:24; compare 11:13, which sets “altars to the shameful thing” beside “altars to burn incense to Baal”), and ends in lying down in shame and acknowledging sin “from our youth even to this day” (3:25). Readers differ on whether this liturgy shows the repentance the LORD desires, voiced in advance, or an ideal not yet reached by Judah; 4:1–4 follows with conditions. Classical Arminian and Reformed readers share the conviction that God’s healing and the people’s returning belong together; they differ on whether the returning is a grace-enabled response that could be refused or the fruit of grace that effectively turns the heart (compare 31:18, “Turn me, and I will be turned”).

verses.text: “But I said, ‘How I desire to put you among the children, and give you a pleasant land, a goodly heritage of the armies of the nations!’ and I said, ‘You shall call me “My Father”, and shall not turn away from following me.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says “How I desire to put you among the children” and expected that they would call him “My Father” and not turn away. Arminian readers see a sincere divine longing that Israel’s choices frustrated, consistent with grace that can be resisted (compare the discussion at Deuteronomy 5:29), while God remains faithful to his purposes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s revealed desire for his people’s faithfulness, distinguished from his secret purpose, and note that God alone can secure a people who will not turn away (compare 32:40). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as heartfelt covenant love and hold that Israel’s turning away is her own fault, not God’s.

verses.text: “Surely as a wife treacherously departs from her husband, so you have dealt treacherously with me, house of Israel,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD compares the house of Israel to a wife who treacherously departs from her husband. Arminian readers see covenant treachery as a real betrayal of a relationship that God entered in good faith, which only makes sense if Israel could have remained faithful by grace and freely chose otherwise.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the marriage image underscoring both the intimacy of God’s covenant and the gravity of sin against it, which is relational before it is legal. Shared ground: both traditions keep the image sober and covenantal, and both hear the LORD’s personal grief in the words “you have dealt treacherously with me.”

verses.text: A voice is heard on the bare heights, the weeping and the petitions of the children of Israel; because they have perverted their way, they have forgotten the LORD their God.
verses.arminianNotes: A voice is heard on the bare heights, the weeping and petitions of the children of Israel, because they have perverted their way and forgotten the LORD. Arminian readers see the beginning of genuine sorrow at the very sites of idolatry, the place where the call of grace now meets a people starting to respond.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that weeping may begin as distress before it becomes repentance, and that the LORD’s call in the next verse supplies what weeping cannot. Shared ground: both traditions read the bare heights as an ironic setting (3:2), and both see forgetting the LORD as the root of the people’s perverted way.

verses.text: Return, you backsliding children, and I will heal your backsliding. “Behold, we have come to you; for you are the LORD our God.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD calls, “Return … and I will heal your backsliding,” and the people answer, “Behold, we have come to you.” Arminian readers see prevenient grace calling and enabling, the people responding, and the LORD healing those who return. The order in the verse, call, response, healing, reflects a cooperative relationship of grace and faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hear in “I will heal your backsliding” the LORD’s pledge to cure the very disease of turning away, which includes the turning itself (compare 31:18, “Turn me, and I will be turned”). Shared ground: both traditions affirm that the call is sincere, that the people truly come, and that healing is the LORD’s gracious work.

verses.text: Truly help from the hills, the tumult on the mountains, is in vain. Truly the salvation of Israel is in the LORD our God.
verses.arminianNotes: The people confess that help from the hills and the tumult on the mountains is in vain, and that Israel’s salvation is in the LORD. Arminian readers see repentance as a real renunciation: turning to God includes turning from false trusts, and the people’s confession shows the kind of response grace invites from everyone.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the confession as the true knowledge of God that grace produces: salvation belongs to the LORD alone and no rival source can supply it. Shared ground: both traditions read the hills and mountains as places of idolatrous worship, and both treat “the salvation of Israel is in the LORD our God” as the confession at the center.

verses.text: But the shameful thing has devoured the labor of our fathers from our youth, their flocks and their herds, their sons and their daughters.
verses.arminianNotes: The people say that “the shameful thing” has devoured their fathers’ labor, flocks, herds, sons, and daughters. Many readers take “the shameful thing” as a deliberate way of referring to Baal (compare 11:13). Arminian readers see repentance tracing sin’s costs honestly, including losses inherited from earlier generations’ choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the confession acknowledging that idolatry is not only wrong but destructive, consuming what God gave. They also note that the mention of sons and daughters may recall child sacrifice condemned elsewhere (7:31), though this is not certain here. Shared ground: both traditions see the people naming sin and its costs without excuse.

verses.text: Let us lie down in our shame, and let our confusion cover us; for we have sinned against the LORD our God, we and our fathers, from our youth even to this day. We have not obeyed the LORD our God’s voice.”
verses.arminianNotes: The people lie down in shame, confessing that they and their fathers have sinned from their youth and have not obeyed the LORD’s voice. Arminian readers see genuine repentance as owning both personal and corporate sin, and note that the confession sets the stage for the conditional promises of 4:1–2, which call for a lived response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in this confession the honest self-knowledge that accompanies true conversion, sin acknowledged as pervasive and long-standing. Some read it as the confession God desires rather than one Judah actually made. Shared ground: both traditions read 3:25 as a model of humble confession, and both see shame here as leading toward the LORD.
